section.title: Israel's Wickedness Exposed
section.sectionRationale: God moves from what He desires to what He sees when He looks to heal Israel: deceit, palace intrigue, and burning passions for evil. The chapter piles up vivid images, an overheated oven, a half-baked cake, a senseless dove, a faulty bow, to show a people whose whole life has turned away from the LORD.
section.thesis: When God would heal Israel, He instead uncovers a nation on fire with evil and self-deceived in its decline, courting Egypt and Assyria yet never crying out to God from the heart.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the exposed corruption of court and country; the oven of passions that consumes rulers and kings; and the senseless dove that flits between empires but will not return to the Most High.

units.label: When I would heal, iniquity appears

verses.text: When I {{rapha|heal}} Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim will be exposed, as well as the crimes of Samaria. For they practice deceit and thieves break in; bandits raid in the streets.
But they fail to consider in their hearts that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds are all around them; they are before My face.

units.label: The oven of their passions
units.note: hearts hot for evil, kings falling

verses.text: They delight the king with their evil, and the princes with their lies.
They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by a baker who needs not stoke the fire from the kneading to the rising of the dough.
The princes are inflamed with wine on the day of our king; so he joins hands with those who mock him.
For they prepare their heart like an oven while they lie in wait; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire.
All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings fall; not one of them calls upon Me.

units.label: A cake unturned, a dove without sense

verses.text: Ephraim mixes with the nations; Ephraim is an unturned cake.
Foreigners consume his strength, but he does not notice. Even his hair is streaked with gray, but he does not know.
Israel’s arrogance testifies against them, yet they do not return to the LORD their God; despite all this, they do not seek Him.
So Ephraim has become like a silly, senseless {{yonah|dove}}, calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria.
As they go, I will spread My net over them; I will bring them down like birds of the air. I will chastise them when I hear them flocking together.
Woe to them, for they have strayed from Me! Destruction to them, for they have rebelled against Me! Though I would {{padah|redeem}} them, they speak lies against Me.
They do not cry out to Me from their hearts when they wail upon their beds. They slash themselves for grain and new wine, but turn away from Me.
Although I trained and strengthened their arms, they plot evil against Me.
They turn, but not to the Most High; they are like a faulty bow. Their leaders will fall by the sword for the cursing of their tongue; for this they will be ridiculed in the land of Egypt.

rapha.gloss: To heal, to cure, to restore. A key word in Hosea for what God longs to do for His people, from He will heal us in chapter 6 to I will heal their apostasy in chapter 14. Here the tragedy is that when God moves to heal, He uncovers festering iniquity instead of a heart ready to be made well.

yonah.gloss: A dove or pigeon. Here it pictures Ephraim as a silly, senseless bird, easily lured and flitting anxiously between Egypt and Assyria. The image mocks Israel's foreign policy: instead of resting in the LORD, they flutter fearfully to empires that cannot save.

padah.gloss: To ransom, to redeem, to buy back, often by paying a price. God says He would redeem His people, but they answer with lies. The word looks ahead to the true redemption God accomplishes in Christ, who ransoms His people not with silver but with His own blood.

basic.context: God turns to heal Israel and instead uncovers a nation rotten to the core: deceit in the streets, plots in the palace, drunken feasts where princes are killed. He compares their passions to a baker's oven that stays hot all night and blazes by morning, so hot that they burn up their own kings. Ephraim is like a half-baked cake, ruined on one side, and like a man going gray without noticing. Worst of all, they flit like a foolish dove between Egypt and Assyria for help, but they never truly cry out to God from the heart.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is a chain of images rather than a single argument, each one exposing a facet of Israel's decline: moral, political, and spiritual. The repeated note is self-deception, they do not notice, do not know, do not consider. The oracle assumes God's genuine desire to heal and redeem, which makes the people's refusal all the more tragic.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with God's wish to rapha, heal, His people. It mocks Ephraim as a yonah, a silly dove, flitting to Egypt and Assyria. And it records God's astonishing willingness to padah, redeem, His people, met only with lies. Heal, redeem: these are gospel words spurned by a self-deceived nation.
basic.typology: God's frustrated desire to heal and redeem a people who will not cry out to Him from the heart sets in relief the work of Christ, who both accomplishes the redemption and creates in His people the crying heart that turns to God. The kings who fall because none calls on the LORD point to the need for the true King who always does the Father's will.
basic.christ: Here God says, I would redeem them, but they speak lies against Me. In Christ that thwarted longing becomes accomplished fact: the Son ransoms His people not with silver but with His own blood, and gives them a new heart that cries Abba, Father. Where Israel turned but not to the Most High, Jesus is the one who always turned wholly to God, and by His Spirit He teaches His people to cry out from the heart at last.
basic.god: God searches hearts and remembers every deed; nothing is hidden before His face. Yet the chapter reveals a God who wants to heal and redeem, grieved by a people who will not come. He is patient, having trained and strengthened Israel, and just, for persistent rebellion will meet the net and the sword. His anger here is the wounded love of a spurned healer.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 1:18 says we are redeemed not with silver but with the precious blood of Christ. Romans 8:15 speaks of the Spirit by whom we cry Abba, Father. Psalm 78 recounts a people who flattered God with their mouths but whose hearts were not loyal.
basic.oneStory: Chapter 7 shows a God eager to heal and redeem, refused by a self-deceived people who cry to everyone but Him. The gospel answers this in Christ, who redeems His people at the cost of His blood and gives them hearts that truly cry out to God.

context.literary:
Hosea 7 begins by finishing a sentence. The last verse of chapter 6 said, 'when I restore My people from captivity,' and chapter 7 continues, 'When I heal Israel.' The two clauses sound like a physician reaching for the wound, and what he finds is rot. God's healing does not make the sickness vanish; it exposes it, 'the iniquity of Ephraim will be exposed, as well as the crimes of Samaria,' verse 1. The chapter is therefore a diagnosis made at the moment of treatment.

It is built from a chain of pictures, in three clusters. Verses 1 to 7 are about the palace and are held together by the oven, which appears in verses 4, 6 and 7: a baker's fire that smoulders through the night and blazes at dawn. Verses 8 to 12 turn to foreign policy and use bread and birds, the unturned cake in verse 8, the silly dove in verse 11, and the hunter's net in verse 12. Verses 13 to 16 turn to the heart, with the cry 'Woe to them' at the opening, God's yearning, 'Though I would redeem them,' and the final image of a faulty bow.

A refrain runs underneath: failure to turn or call. 'Not one of them calls upon Me,' verse 7. 'They do not return to the LORD their God,' verse 10. 'They do not cry out to Me from their hearts,' verse 14. 'They turn, but not to the Most High,' verse 16. Each of these sentences is a negative where a verb of prayer would be expected. Meanwhile the people are very active: they scheme, drink, mix with the nations, flutter to Egypt, wail on their beds. Hosea's point is that all of this motion is a substitute for the one movement that would help.

The second thing to notice is the repeated 'they do not know,' verses 2, 9. The nation is sick and unaware, and the unawareness is part of the sickness.
context.historical:
The details of the chapter fit the final decades of the northern kingdom. After Jeroboam II, Israel had six kings in about thirty years, and four of them were killed by conspirators. Shallum struck down Zechariah in front of the people, 2 Kings 15:10. Menahem went up from Tirzah and killed Shallum, 2 Kings 15:14. Pekah, with fifty men of Gilead, murdered Pekahiah in the citadel of the king's palace, 2 Kings 15:25, and Hoshea killed Pekah, 2 Kings 15:30. That is the world of verse 7: 'They devour their rulers. All their kings fall; not one of them calls upon Me.'

Verse 5 mentions 'the day of our king,' probably an anniversary of the king's accession or birthday. Such feasts are known elsewhere, as when Pharaoh held a feast on his birthday, Genesis 40:20. In this picture the court is drunk, the king is lured into mockery, and the plotters use the party as cover. The oven is a household image, since a baker would bank the fire at night and stir it up in the morning, and the footnote's 'their baker sleeps' fits a conspiracy that waits, quiet and hot, until the right moment.

The flitting of the dove in verse 11 describes a foreign policy with no fixed point. Menahem paid Assyria, 2 Kings 15:19, and Hoshea, who owed tribute to Assyria, sent envoys to King So of Egypt, which led to his arrest, 2 Kings 17:4. Jeremiah later says Judah would be disappointed by Egypt just as by Assyria, Jeremiah 2:36.

The ritual in verse 14 was a common feature of the Baal cult. When Elijah faced the prophets of Baal on Carmel, they 'cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom,' 1 Kings 18:28. Hosea 2:8 had said that Israel did not acknowledge that it was the LORD who gave grain, new wine and oil. So when they slash themselves for grain and wine in chapter 7, they are going to the wrong supplier. The jab in verse 16 that they will be ridiculed in Egypt is bitter, since Egypt is where they had hoped to find help.
context.canonical:
The chapter's themes are among the commonest in the prophets. The unstable nation that runs from one great power to another appears in Isaiah's warning, 'Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help,' Isaiah 31:1-3, and in Jeremiah's, 'How unstable you are, constantly changing your ways! You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria,' Jeremiah 2:36. Hosea himself comes back to the point in 12:1 and 14:3. The failing monarchy is the subject of Hosea 13:10-11, where God says He gave a king in anger and took him away in wrath, and behind it stands the warning of 1 Samuel 8 that a human king would take more than he gave.

The phrase 'I would redeem them' sits within a long tradition about God as redeemer. The first redemption was the exodus, 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm,' Exodus 6:6, and Deuteronomy 7:8 recalls that He 'redeemed you from the house of slavery.' The Psalter adds the hope that 'with Him is redemption in abundance,' and that He will redeem Israel from all his iniquities, Psalm 130:7-8. By saying 'I would redeem them' in the face of lies, Hosea 7:13 puts Israel in the position of Egypt's former slaves who are given every offer of deliverance and who refuse.

The cry in verse 14 'from their hearts' echoes the whole Bible's understanding of prayer. The psalms teach the people to pour out their hearts before God, Psalm 62:8, and the stories of the Judges show that cry as the hinge of salvation, 'when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up' a deliverer, Judges 3:9. Hosea hears the sound of wailing and finds it is not that cry.

In the New Testament the redeeming verb is the language of the gospel: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and 'He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness,' Titus 2:14. Zechariah's song begins, 'He has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68. Paul says that 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' Romans 10:13, the open door that Hosea's people refused.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea meant to wake the sleepers. The most striking thing about this chapter is how often the people do not notice. 'They fail to consider in their hearts that I remember all their evil,' verse 2. 'Foreigners consume his strength, but he does not notice,' verse 9. 'Even his hair is streaked with gray, but he does not know.' The nation has grown old and sapped without once checking itself in the mirror. A prophet's job in such a moment is not to supply new information but to make the obvious visible, and the pictures of the half-baked cake and the grey hair are exactly that.

He wanted them to understand that the troubles of the palace and the troubles of the shrine were one trouble. The princes who 'are inflamed with wine' and the people who 'wail upon their beds' are alike in this: neither is calling on God. Political chaos was not a separate subject from unfaith but its symptom.

He wanted them to hear God's own wish to heal and redeem. The chapter begins with a physician and ends with a bow that fails to shoot straight, but in its middle is one of the most startling lines in the book, 'Though I would redeem them, they speak lies against Me.' A people who thought of God as only angry needed to hear that He was willing.

And he wanted them to stop running. The dove's flight from Egypt to Assyria is a picture of a nation exhausted by its own anxiety, and the stern answer is that it is flying into a net that He Himself spreads. The only escape from that net is to turn, not to Egypt or Assyria, but to Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records the political and religious state of Israel in its last decades. It does not endorse conspiracies, drunken feasts or the policy of playing one empire against another, and it does not lay down a program for how a modern nation should handle its alliances. The images are Hosea's own and are given to a particular people at a particular time. We should be careful about drawing a straight line from Israel to any modern country, which is not a covenant people in the same way.

What is meant to carry over is the way people behave when they will not turn to God, and the ways in which sin deadens perception. Many of the verbs are about not noticing, and the warning is relevant to individuals, congregations and nations alike. Being worn down without feeling the loss is a hazard for every generation.

The line about wailing on beds without crying out to God from the heart is a call to examine prayer. It does not condemn grief or lament, which fill the Psalms, but it does show that loud distress is not the same as turning to God. In the same way, God's wish to redeem, 'Though I would redeem them,' is not an invitation to presume. The point of the sentence is that He is willing, and the response it calls for is to come, not to assume that because He is willing nothing needs to change.

Finally, the chapter should not be turned into a general ban on politics or on seeking help from others. Hosea's complaint is against help sought in place of the LORD, by those who 'do not seek Him,' verse 10.

debates.question: What is the oven image of verses 4 to 7 describing?

views.label: A plot to assassinate the king
views.case: The context supplies the setting of the royal drinking party in verse 5 and ends with 'they devour their rulers,' verse 7. The baker who stops stoking the fire, or sleeps, is the conspirator who waits through the night until the king is at his weakest, and the dawn blaze is the coup. Many readers take it this way because it matches the pattern of Shallum, Menahem and Pekah in 2 Kings 15.

views.label: The moral and spiritual heat of the whole nation
views.case: The first line of verse 4 calls them all adulterers, and the picture is of lust and passion that burns without need of fuel. On this reading the oven is a general image for uncontrolled desire in the people, and the royal events are the most visible outcome.

views.label: A combination
views.case: Other readers see the Hebrew of these verses as a difficult text and think the picture moves between the plotters and the king's own folly, so that the baker could be either the plotter or the careless ruler. The footnote that the Hebrew says 'their baker sleeps' shows how uncertain the details are.

debates.bearing: The details of the Hebrew are hard, and a firm choice is not needed to hear the point: a nation whose heart is burning with the wrong passions will consume its own leaders, and 'not one of them calls upon Me.'

debates.question: Do they 'slash themselves' or 'gather together' in verse 14?

views.label: They slash themselves, as Baal's prophets did
views.case: The BSB follows some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint, as the footnote says, and links the line to 1 Kings 18:28, where Baal's prophets cut themselves. The setting is a cult ritual for grain and wine. Hosea's charge is then that they have gone to Baal for what the LORD gives.

views.label: They gather together for grain and wine
views.case: Most Hebrew manuscripts read a different verb, and the footnote says 'They gather together.' That sense also works. They assemble to ask for harvest, in wailing and prayer, but with no heart for God, which fits 'do not cry out to Me from their hearts.'

debates.bearing: Both readings make the same point about motive: the people want grain and wine, not God. The first reading gives a vivid picture of how far they had gone, but the argument of the verse does not depend on it.

study.originalLanguages:
The oven of verse 4 is the tannur, the clay oven used in every household. The people are called adulterers, from the verb na'aph, 'to commit adultery,' and the oven is the picture of what that passion is like. The picture works because bread rises on the heat that adultery generates: the baker has only to keep it banked, and the fire does the rest. The word is the same as in Hosea 3:1, where Hosea is told to love a woman who is 'an adulteress.' The marriage imagery stays active in the middle of a political chapter.

In verse 8 Ephraim is 'an unturned cake.' The noun is ugah, a round flat loaf baked on hot stones or coals, and the participle 'unturned,' hafukhah, is the picture of bread left on one side. Such a loaf burns on the bottom and stays raw on top, which is useless for eating. The verb before it, rendered 'mixes,' has the sense of being stirred into a mixture, and it describes Ephraim thoroughly blended with the nations until nothing distinctive remains.

The dove of verse 11 is 'silly,' pothah, from a verb meaning to be open or easily persuaded. The related adjective describes the simple man who 'believes every word,' Proverbs 14:15. The next word, 'senseless,' is literally 'without heart,' ein lev, and in Hebrew the heart is the seat of understanding. A dove which has no sense is no more than a bird that goes where it is driven.

The two forms of discipline in verses 12 and 15 are worth hearing together. 'I will chastise them' in verse 12 and 'I trained' in verse 15 come from the same root, yasar, the verb for correcting and instructing as a father does. God says He trained their arms and strengthened them, and they turned that strength on Him. The same verb can mean to teach and to correct, which is why Psalm 94:12 says that the man God disciplines is blessed. Hosea's God has done both, and has been repaid with plots.

The 'net' of verse 12 is resheth, a bird catcher's or hunter's net. The one in whom the dove trusts is the one who spreads it. The picture was not new, and the point is that the bird thinks it is flying free.

In verse 14 the people 'wail,' yalal, the verb of howling in grief or distress, on their beds. The form is a cry of pain, and the complaint is that it is the wrong cry. The corresponding verb for calling, za'aq, is the one used when Israel 'cried out' in Judges 3:9, and Hosea's accusation is that they howl but do not cry out.

Last, the 'faulty bow' of verse 16 is the qesheth remiyyah, a bow that slackens or deceives. Psalm 78:57 uses the same phrase of the earlier generation: 'twisted like a faulty bow.' It is a weapon that looks right and fails when it matters, and the arrow flies off to the side.

typology.type: The redeemer who would redeem, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: 'Though I would redeem them' recalls the exodus, when God redeemed Israel from slavery, Exodus 6:6, and Hosea's generation had been offered that same redeeming love and turned it down. In Christ the redemption is carried out at the highest price. 'The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and 'it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed... but with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18. The type falls short in that the exodus freed a nation from Pharaoh, while Christ frees His people from lawlessness itself, Titus 2:14.

typology.type: The kings who fall, one after another, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The line of Israel's last kings is a chain of assassinations. The true King, in contrast, 'will reign on the throne of David... to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore,' Isaiah 9:7. He does not climb to power by plot; He tells Pilate, 'My kingdom is not of this world,' John 18:36, and is raised to a throne by the Father. The pattern runs by contrast: the plotter takes a throne by killing the king, and Christ takes His by being killed. The type fails to reach the point where the King's death is itself the saving act.

typology.type: Wailing on beds and the cry from the heart, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: Hosea contrasts the howl of the self-interested with a cry that comes from the heart. Hebrews tells us that in the days of His earthly life Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. His praying is the true cry that the nation could not make. And the people of God now share it: 'you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!' Romans 8:15. The type breaks down at the source of the cry, which is not the heart's effort but the Spirit's gift.

study.christ:
Hosea 7 leads to Christ most directly by the verb in verse 13, 'Though I would redeem them.' The sentence is half finished: the 'would' hangs, because Israel refuses. In the New Testament it is completed. 'He has visited and redeemed His people,' sings Zechariah at the birth of John, Luke 1:68. The ransom that was offered and rejected is paid. 'He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession,' Titus 2:14. The longing of the God who wished to redeem finds its deed in the Son, who 'did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Peter reminds believers that the price was not 'silver or gold' but 'the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19.

It leads to Christ by the first word of the chapter, 'When I heal Israel.' The God who wants to heal is the God who sends the Physician, and Matthew says that when Jesus healed the sick it was to fulfil Isaiah, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17. Hosea's complaint is that the sickness is not noticed, and Jesus' word is that the Physician is for those who know they are sick.

It leads to Christ by contrast of heart. Hosea says that Israel does not cry out 'from their hearts.' Jesus is the one who does. In Gethsemane and on the cross He prayed with loud cries and tears, and was heard, Hebrews 5:7. He is the Israelite who turns, wholly, to the Most High, in the place where Israel turned 'but not to the Most High.' And by His Spirit He makes that cry the ordinary speech of His people, 'Abba! Father!' Romans 8:15. What Israel could not do in its own strength is given as a gift.

It leads to Christ by the contrast of kingship. The kings of Israel were killed by those who wished to take their places. This King says, 'My kingdom is not of this world,' John 18:36, and goes willingly to death. His throne is secure because it is not taken by force, and because He lives.

And it leads to Him by the gospel's open door: 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' Romans 10:13. Hosea 7:7 and 7:14 are the negative of this; Romans 10 is the positive. The refusal that makes a nation sink is the very thing the gospel invites each person to reverse.

As always, there is a limit. The chapter does not name the Messiah, and the oven, the cake and the dove are not hidden pictures of Jesus. What it provides is an accurate account of the problem, a God who wishes to redeem, and a gap that Christ fills.
study.god:
The chapter begins with a God who wishes to heal, and it is worth lingering over this, because the rest of the chapter is so harsh. The wish to heal comes first. God does not enter the scene looking for something to punish; He enters as a physician, and the punishments follow because the patient will not hold still. The same longing is behind verse 13: 'Though I would redeem them.' If we want to know what the God of Hosea is like, we should start there.

He is a God who remembers. 'I remember all their evil,' verse 2, is said to people who have forgotten. Their deeds are 'all around them; they are before My face.' Nothing in the nation's past has been lost. This is a threat, but it is also the other side of His faithfulness, since the God who remembers sin is the God who remembers promises.

He is patient and a trainer. 'I trained and strengthened their arms,' verse 15, shows the picture of a father teaching a boy to use a bow. The strength with which they plot against Him was His gift. This turns the reader's attention from the sin to the kindness it abuses, and from the sin to the grief of a father.

He is just. The net in verse 12 is a form of judgment. He will bring the dove down 'when I hear them flocking together.' The punishment fits the offence, since a people that runs to nations for refuge finds those nations are a trap. The leaders who cursed with their tongues are to fall by the sword, and the very Egypt they courted will laugh at them, verse 16.

He is not deceived by performance. They wail on their beds, they slash themselves for grain and wine, and He sees that their hearts are not toward Him. The God who accepts tears is the God who can tell which tears are prayers.

And He is the Lord of the nations. Egypt and Assyria appear as places to which the dove flies, but He spreads the net over both. The chapter does not set the great powers beside Him as rivals.

For worship, the chapter calls us to bring Him our real distress as prayer and not as noise, to take the fact that He remembers as a reason for honesty, and to hear in 'Though I would redeem them' the standing offer of the God who has not given up.

crossReferences.note: The record of the assassinations behind verse 7. Shallum kills Zechariah, Menahem kills Shallum, Pekah kills Pekahiah, Hoshea kills Pekah. Reading it beside Hosea shows that the prophet is not exaggerating when he says that 'all their kings fall,' and that nobody calls on God.

Hoshea sends envoys to King So of Egypt and stops paying tribute to Assyria, and the king of Assyria arrests him. It is the fulfilment of the dove's flight in verse 11: a last attempt to turn to Egypt, at the time when Samaria is about to fall.

Jeremiah applies the same charge to Judah a century later: 'How unstable you are, constantly changing your ways! You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria.' The two prophets together show that the habit of trusting the great powers was not an Israelite accident but a long pattern.

The prophets of Baal on Carmel cry louder and cut themselves with knives and lances until the blood gushes, and there is no answer. The scene explains the footnote of Hosea 7:14, and shows how little Baal's frantic ritual achieved compared with a quiet word to the LORD.

God says Israel did not acknowledge that it was He who gave the grain, new wine and oil. This is the backdrop of Hosea 7:14, where they slash themselves for the same grain and wine. The gifts were God's all along, and they looked for them from a false source.

The same phrase, a faulty bow, is applied to the generation that was faithless like their fathers. It sets Hosea 7:16 in a long line of those who looked like Israel but were unreliable at the moment of need.

The first promise of redemption: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm.' It shows what 'redeem' meant for Israel from the start, an act of God's strength on behalf of slaves. Hosea 7:13 shows that the same God was still offering it.

The Psalmist hopes that Israel will wait for the LORD, because with Him is redemption in abundance, and He will redeem Israel from all his iniquities. It is the answer to Hosea 7:13: the redemption that was refused is the one that finally comes.

Isaiah's woe to those who go to Egypt for help because they trust in horses and not in the Holy One of Israel. His argument, that the Egyptians are men and not God, gives the reasoning behind Hosea's mockery of the silly dove.

Jesus' prayers with loud cries and tears are the cry from the heart that Hosea 7:14 says is missing. He is heard because of His reverence, and His heard cry is the ground for those who now cry out in His name.

'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' It is the counterpoint to the refrain of Hosea 7, where no one calls on Him. The simple offer is the same, and the response is the difference.

Christ gave Himself to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify a people for His own possession. The redemption God wished for in Hosea 7:13 is accomplished here, and its purpose is a people who are zealous for good deeds, the opposite of Israel's plots.

study.oneStory:
Hosea 7 stands in the long story of how humanity tries to rescue itself. Genesis 3 began with a couple who sewed fig leaves and hid. Babel in Genesis 11 was a unified effort to make a name. In Hosea 7 the same instinct is at work in a nation: politics as self-rescue, alliances as self-protection, ritual as self-service. In each case the project fails, and the thing from which it flees comes to it.

The chapter is also part of the long story of Israel and Egypt. The exodus was the first redemption, and the law forbade the king to send people back to Egypt, 'You are never to go back that way again,' Deuteronomy 17:16. Now Israel flutters toward Egypt in a panic, and Hosea warns elsewhere that they will return there, Hosea 8:13 and 9:3. A nation that was brought out of slavery is returning by its own choice to the house of slavery, and the reversal is the sign of how far it has moved from the God who redeemed it.

The theme of kingship is likewise a thread through the Bible. The people asked for a king like the nations, and 1 Samuel 8 warned what it would cost. Hosea 7 shows the result at the end of the line, kings killing kings and no one calling on God, and Hosea 13:10 asks where those kings are now. This is the problem for which the promise of a different King is the answer.

Hosea's words about redemption look ahead. In the Gospels, God comes to heal and redeem in the Person of His Son, who gives His life as a ransom, and sends His Spirit so that His people cry 'Abba! Father!' The cry that Hosea could not find is put into the mouths of the redeemed.

The story ends with the healing that Hosea wished for. In the new creation 'the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. Those who were purchased by the blood of the Lamb from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, Revelation 5:9, stand before the throne, and the Spirit and the bride say 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The nation that never called is replaced by a people who do, and the God who said 'Though I would redeem them' finds them at last willing.

quiz.q: What does God find when He moves to heal Israel?

options.text: Festering iniquity, deceit, and crime, exposed rather than cured.
options.note: Verse 1 says the iniquity of Ephraim is exposed when God would heal.

options.text: A people already fully repentant.
options.note: The opposite is true; their sin is uncovered, not healed.

options.text: A nation too poor to sin much.
options.note: Their wickedness is abundant, not limited by poverty.

options.text: Perfect faithfulness among the priests.
options.note: Corruption reaches the palace and the whole people.

quiz.q: What does the image of a silly, senseless dove describe?

options.text: Israel fluttering fearfully between Egypt and Assyria instead of resting in the LORD.
options.note: Verse 11 pictures Ephraim calling to Egypt then turning to Assyria.

options.text: Israel's gentleness and innocence.
options.note: The dove here means foolishness, not innocence.

options.text: Israel's peaceful trust in God.
options.note: It pictures the opposite, faithless trust in foreign powers.

options.text: Israel's military strength.
options.note: It mocks their weakness and folly, not their strength.

quiz.q: What is the tragic refrain running through the chapter?

options.text: They do not notice, do not know, and do not cry out to God from the heart.
options.note: Verses 9, 10, and 14 all stress their self-deception and heartlessness.

options.text: They cry out to God constantly and sincerely.
options.note: They wail on their beds but not from the heart to God.

options.text: They keep the law perfectly.
options.note: They plot evil and rebel, far from keeping the law.

options.text: They have forgotten how to speak.
options.note: They speak plenty, including lies against God; they will not turn to Him.

quiz.q: How does God's frustrated desire to redeem point to Christ?

options.text: What Israel refused, Christ accomplishes, redeeming His people with His blood and giving them hearts that cry to God.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:18 and Romans 8:15 show the redemption fulfilled.

options.text: It proves God gave up on redemption entirely.
options.note: God's desire to redeem is fulfilled, not abandoned, in Christ.

options.text: It shows redemption depends on Israel's silver.
options.note: True redemption is by Christ's blood, not silver.

options.text: It has no link to Christ.
options.note: Redeem is a gospel word fulfilled in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does turning, but not to the Most High, teach?

options.text: Half-hearted, misdirected turning is not true repentance; only a whole turning to God will do.
options.note: Verse 16 exposes a turning that misses God like a faulty bow.

options.text: Any kind of turning is good enough.
options.note: The chapter shows a turning that still misses God entirely.

options.text: God accepts turning to Egypt as well as to Himself.
options.note: Turning to Egypt is precisely the folly condemned.

options.text: Repentance is impossible for anyone.
options.note: True return is possible and desired; in Christ it is given.

questions: God saw Israel going gray without noticing its own decline. Where might you be losing spiritual strength without realizing it?
The people cried out on their beds but not to God from the heart. What is the difference between complaining about your troubles and truly crying out to God?
Ephraim trusted Egypt and Assyria rather than the LORD. What earthly powers or plans do you flit to for security instead of resting in God?
God said, I would redeem them, but they speak lies against Me. How does it move you that God's desire to redeem is fulfilled for you in Christ?
Israel turned, but not to the Most High. Is there an area where your turning is half-hearted or aimed at the wrong thing, and what would a whole turning to God look like?

translationNotes.note: All night their anger smolders reflects a reading of the Hebrew; the source note observes the literal their baker sleeps, picturing the oven left to build heat overnight.
I will chastise them when I hear them flocking together may also be rendered I will chastise them according to what was reported against them in the assembly.
They slash themselves follows some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint, compare 1 Kings 18:28; most Hebrew manuscripts read they gather together.
